citation: Communal farmers' cattle-production perceptions, Ga-Matlala, Limpopo (PMC)
Livestock ownership determinants, OR Tambo District (Pastoralism, Springer)
Drought coping strategies and livestock resilience in SA (PMC)
mechanisms: Cattle are kept as a liquid asset for large expenses and inheritance, so any intervention that demands cash outlay is rejected unless it directly protects that income role.
Cattle theft is read as a symptom of youth unemployment and absent herders, so a solution is credible only if it absorbs idle youth labour or substitutes for the missing herder.

A household will own a livestock species only if its perceived utility—income, food, or cultural role—outweighs that of alternatives, so a new policy is judged by whether it lifts the utility of the species the household already prefers.

Resilience to drought depends on access to diverse resources, social networks, and finance, so a policy is seen as building resilience only if it widens those three channels; otherwise it is dismissed as inadequate.
objection_patterns: Does this require me to spend cash that I would otherwise keep in my cattle?
Does this give the unemployed youth a reason to stop stealing my cattle?
Does this make the species I already keep more useful to my household?
Does this give me access to finance or a network that I can lean on when drought hits?
confidence: Mixed-methods and survey-based, three study areas across Limpopo and Eastern Cape — mechanisms are consistent across contexts, but magnitudes and precise regional boundaries are not quantified.
